proof:
# A centered slab-tail packing inequality for every concavity degree

Let `d>=1` be real. Let `(w_i)` be a nonzero nonnegative sequence on a finite consecutive integer interval, and suppose `(w_i^(1/d))` is concave there. Assume its weighted integer mean is zero:

\[
\sum_i i w_i=0.
\]

Put `M=sum w_i`, `m=max w_i`, and define

\[
r_d=\left(\frac{2}{d+2}\right)^{(d+1)/d},\qquad
\kappa_d=\frac1{3+d r_d}.
\tag{1}
\]

Then for every integer `h>=0`,

\[
\boxed{\quad
\sum_{i>h}w_i\ge\kappa_d[M-(2h+1)m],\qquad
\sum_{i<-h}w_i\ge\kappa_d[M-(2h+1)m].\quad}
\tag{2}
\]

The constants satisfy

\[
\frac15<\kappa_d\le\frac9{31}<\frac3{10},
\qquad \lim_{d\to\infty}\kappa_d=\frac15.
\]

For `d=1` the separate elementary theorem in `candidate ad8324f468564d7c` improves this constant to `1/3`. The point here is an all-degree extension of the **slab-tail** estimate. It does not address oblique mixed caps in higher continuous dimension.

## 1. The exact existing tail inputs

Remove zero endpoint terms. Positive terms remain a consecutive interval `[l,r]`, retain their mass and mean, and retain root concavity. For the actual suffixes

\[
F_j=\sum_{i=j}^r w_i,\qquad l\le j\le r,
\]

the all-degree arithmetic-increment proof in `candidate 821242aee5d2f3e1` establishes that

\[
F_j^{\beta}\ \text{is concave on its actual indices},
\qquad \beta=\frac1{d+1}.
\tag{3}
\]

Its Jensen and upper-endpoint Riemann-sum consequence at the integer mean gives

\[
F_0\ge\left(\frac{d+1}{d+2}\right)^{d+1}M>\frac M3.
\tag{4}
\]

The last elementary bound holds also for real `d`: `(1+1/(d+1))^(d+1)<=e<3`. For example `e<3` follows from the factorial series and `k!>=2^(k-1)` for `k>=2`, with a strict inequality at `k=3`. Neither (3) nor (4) inserts a concavity condition at the artificial suffix `F_(r+1)=0`.

Two estimates used below are recorded explicitly. First, if all actual decrements `F_j^beta-F_(j+1)^beta` from an index `s<r` onward are at least `c>0`, then, writing `T=F_s`,

\[
E:=\sum_{i\ge s}(i-s+1)w_i
\le T+\frac{T^{1+\beta}}{(d+2)c}.
\tag{5}
\]

Indeed `F_(s+v)<=(T^beta-vc)_+^(d+1)` on actual suffix indices by addition of the decrements, and after the support its left side is zero. Summing suffixes and bounding the terms after `v=0` by the integral of this decreasing nonnegative function proves (5). With only one tail term, `E=T` and all subsequent displayed upper bounds remain true without defining a final decrement.

Second, for mass `A` on integers at most `h`, with each entry at most `m`, the first moment is at most

\[
hA-\frac{A^2}{2m}+\frac A2.
\tag{6}
\]

This is exact discrete packing: writing `A=qm+s`, `0<=s<m`, filling the nearest `q` sites with mass `m` and the next with mass `s` minimizes distance to `h`. Its distance exceeds `A^2/(2m)-A/2` by `s(m-s)/(2m)>=0`.

## 2. Reduction to a small positive right tail

Reflection will give the left inequality, so consider `T=sum_(i>h)w_i`, `k=2h+1`. Suppose, for contradiction,

\[
T<\kappa_d(M-km).
\tag{7}
\]

In particular `M>km`. If `T=0`, apply (6) to the entire sequence; its zero mean gives `M<=km`, a contradiction. Hence `T>0`. Write

\[
t=T/M,\qquad \rho=m/M,\qquad x=k\rho.
\]

Then

\[
0<t<\kappa_d(1-x),\qquad x<1,
\qquad t<\frac3{10}<\frac13.
\tag{8}
\]

The positive support either consists solely of index zero, when (7) is impossible, or has zero strictly between its extreme indices. Put `s=h+1`, an actual positive-support index because `T>0`, and choose a mode `p` with `w_p=m`.

The elementary bounds on `kappa_d` used here are as follows. Since `0<2/(d+2)<1`,
`d r_d<2d/(d+2)<2`, giving `kappa_d>1/5`. Bernoulli's inequality `(3/2)^d>=1+d/2` gives

\[
\left(\frac2{d+2}\right)^{1/d}\ge\frac23,
\quad d r_d\ge\frac{4d}{3(d+2)}\ge\frac49.
\]

Hence `kappa_d<=9/31<3/10`. The limit in the statement follows directly from `d r_d ->2`.

## 3. A mode at or before the tail start

Suppose `p<=s`. If the tail has more than one term, (3) and concavity of the power give

\[
F_s^\beta-F_{s+1}^\beta
\ge F_p^\beta-F_{p+1}^\beta
\ge\frac{m}{(d+1)F_p^{d/(d+1)}}
\ge\frac{m}{(d+1)M^{d/(d+1)}}.
\]

Here `p<=s<r`, so every decrement is an actual one. Subsequent decrements are no smaller. Substitution in (5), also valid as an upper bound in the one-term case, yields

\[
E:=\sum_{i>h}(i-h)w_i
\le T+\frac{d+1}{d+2}
\frac{M^{d/(d+1)}T^{(d+2)/(d+1)}}m.
\tag{9}
\]

Apply (6) to the remaining mass `M-T`. Its first moment plus the tail's first moment `hT+E` is zero. On normalizing this inequality, (9) gives

\[
x\ge(1-t)^2-\rho t
-2\frac{d+1}{d+2}t^{(d+2)/(d+1)}
\ge1-3t+t^2-2\frac{d+1}{d+2}t^{(d+2)/(d+1)},
\tag{10}
\]

where only `rho<=1` was used in the second step.

The function

\[
v\longmapsto v-2\frac{d+1}{d+2}v^{1/(d+1)},\qquad v\ge0,
\]

has its exact global minimum `-d r_d` at `v=r_d`. This follows by differentiating on `v>0`; its derivative is strictly increasing from negative infinity to one, and substituting the unique zero gives the stated value. Thus (10) implies

\[
x\ge1-(3+d r_d)t=1-t/\kappa_d,
\]

contradicting (8).

## 4. A mode strictly after the tail start

Suppose `p>s`. Root concavity implies `w_i<=w_s` for `0<=i<=h`: the root value at `s` is at least each earlier root value by comparison with the maximum at `p`. Consequently (4) gives

\[
(h+1)w_s\ge F_0-T\ge M/3-T>0.
\tag{11}
\]

The initial actual decrement is at least

\[
F_s^\beta-F_{s+1}^\beta
\ge\frac{w_s}{(d+1)T^{d/(d+1)}}.
\]

Using this in (5), then (11), and finally `(d+1)/(d+2)<=1`, gives

\[
E\le T+\frac{d+1}{d+2}\frac{T^2}{w_s}
\le T+\frac{(h+1)T^2}{M/3-T}.
\tag{12}
\]

Packing (6) on the other side and normalizing now yields

\[
x\ge(1-t)^2-\rho t- rac{(x+\rho)t^2}{1/3-t}
\ge(1-t)^2-x t- rac{2x t^2}{1/3-t},
\]

because `rho<=x` for `k>=1`. Therefore

\[
x\ge\frac{(1-t)^2}{1+t+2t^2/(1/3-t)}.
\tag{13}
\]

For every `0<t<3/10`, the right side is strictly larger than `1-10t/3`. Here is the exact verification, with a positive denominator:

\[
(1-t)^2-(1-10t/3)\left(1+t+\frac{2t^2}{1/3-t}\right)
\]
\[
=\frac{t}{3(1/3-t)}
\left(\frac13-\frac83t+7t^2\right)
=\frac{t}{3(1/3-t)}
\left[7(t-4/21)^2+5/63\right]>0.
\]

But (8), together with `kappa_d<3/10`, implies `x<1-10t/3`. This contradicts (13).

Both placements of a mode are exhausted, and zero tails were already handled. This proves the right inequality of (2); reflecting the indices proves the left inequality. Every use of an integral in (5) is an explicit bound on a finite suffix sum, not a replacement of the original integer measure.

## 5. Scope for mixed geometry

The new statement applies directly to a one-dimensional integer marginal whose actual fiber volumes have a concave `d`th root. It bounds the mass remaining beyond a centered integer slab, using the original mean and the maximum actual fiber mass. It can therefore supply captured-tail budgets in a later argument. In dimension `d>1`, the angular derivative of an oblique cap includes varying continuous section measures, so the symmetric proper-index block reduction used for interval fibers does not automatically extend. No such reduction or all-halfspace theorem is assumed here.
